# Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs

Dylan Zhang Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign   
Yanshan Lin Affiliation: IIIS, Tsinghua University, Work done at UIUC   
Zhengkun Wu Affiliation: IIIS, Tsinghua University, Work done at UIUC   
Yihang Sun Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign   
Bingxuan Li Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign   
Dianqi Li Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Hao
Peng Corresponding author: Dylan Zhang;
[shizhuo2@illinois.edu](mailto:shizhuo2@illinois.edu). Project
[Github](https://github.com/DylanZSZ/Memory-Collapse-Eval) Here.
Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

###### Abstract

Learning from past experience benefits from two complementary forms of
memory: _episodic_ traces—raw trajectories of what happened—and
_consolidated_ abstractions distilled across many episodes into
reusable, schema-like lessons. Recent agentic-memory systems pursue the
consolidated form: an LLM rewrites past trajectories into a textual
memory bank that it continuously updates with new interactions,
promising self-improving agents without parameter updates. Yet we find
that such consolidated memories produced by today’s LLMs are often
faulty even when derived from useful experiences. As consolidation
proceeds, memory utility first rises, then degrades, and can fall below
the no-memory baseline. More surprisingly, even when consolidating from
ground-truth solutions, GPT-5.4 fails on 54% of a set of ARC-AGI
problems it had previously solved without memory. We trace the
regression to the consolidation step rather than the underlying
experience: the same trajectories yield qualitatively different memories
under different update schedules, and an episodic-only control that
simply retains those trajectories remains competitive with the
consolidators we test. In a controlled ARC-AGI Stream environment that
exposes Retain, Delete, and Consolidate actions, agents preserve raw
episodes by default and double the accuracy of their
forced-consolidation counterparts; disabling consolidation entirely
(episodic management only) matches this auto regime. Practically, robust
agent memory should treat raw episodes as first-class evidence and gate
consolidation explicitly rather than firing it after every interaction.
Looking forward, reliable agentic memory will require LLMs that can
consolidate without overwriting the evidence they depend on.

## 1 Introduction

Memory consolidation is the cognitive process by which individual
experiences are stabilized, reorganized, and integrated into long-term
memory over time. Rather than preserving every episode as a raw record,
consolidation helps extract recurring patterns, discard incidental
details, and connect new information with existing knowledge. A central
hallmark of intelligence is the ability to turn repeated experience into
reusable knowledge. Humans do not treat every new situation as entirely
unfamiliar; instead, they gradually summarize common structure from past
episodes and organize it into abstractions through memory consolidation
([McClelland et al., 1995](#bib.bib13); [Squire et al.,
2015](#bib.bib1); [Dudai et al., 2015](#bib.bib31); [Moscovitch et al.,
2016](#bib.bib32); [Sun et al., 2023](#bib.bib19); [Bartlett,
1932](#bib.bib2)). These consolidated abstractions allow humans to
transfer lessons learned in one context to novel but related situations,
enabling efficient reasoning, faster adaptation, and more robust
generalization beyond the exact events they have previously encountered.

Recent agentic-memory systems pursue a similar idea for LLM agents.
After solving a problem, an agent can distill its trajectory into a
textual abstraction of the skill it has learned, store this abstraction
in persistent memory, and refine it as more related problems are
encountered ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib18); [Zhao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib6); [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib24); [Sumers et al.,
2024](#bib.bib27); [Park et al., 2023](#bib.bib16); [Majumder et al.,
2023](#bib.bib5); [Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib22); [Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28); [Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib17); [Ouyang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30)). This paradigm is especially appealing because it
suggests a practical path toward self-evolving agents: Experience can be
accumulated, compressed, and reused as compact textual knowledge,
without requiring any parameter updates.

(b) Webshop with AWM.

In this work, we systematically examine what happens when agents
repeatedly compress past trajectories into memory and reuse that memory
over long horizons. To make the experiences themselves informative by
construction, we study settings in which the input trajectories are
demonstrably useful: either drawn from problems the agent has already
solved without memory, or supplied with ground-truth solutions. Even
under these favorable conditions, we find that current LLMs are not
reliable memory consolidators. Each consolidation step is a lossy
rewrite of the memory store: useful details are dropped, spurious rules
are introduced, and once-helpful abstractions drift away from the
underlying task structure. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop ([Yao
et al., 2022](#bib.bib37)), AppWorld ([Trivedi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib39)), and a controlled testbed we introduce to make
consolidation failures more visible, agents that incrementally abstract
their accumulating trajectories into a textual memory bank can briefly
improve or plateau before degrading—in some cases falling below the same
agents without memory at all (Fig.
[1(a)](#S1.F1.sf1 "Figure 1(a) ‣ Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
The clearest case isolates the consolidation step from any input-side
excuse: GPT-5.4 first solves a set of ARC-AGI problems at $`100\%`$
accuracy with no memory; after consolidating from ground-truth solutions
to those very problems, it then fails on $`46\%`$ of them (Fig.
[2](#S1.F2.fig1 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
The failure can therefore be attributed to faulty memory rather than to
noisy trajectories.

Consolidation is fragile in a second sense: the same set of trajectories
can yield qualitatively different memories depending on the order and
grouping of updates. Consolidating the whole trajectory pool in one pass
(Static-All) versus streaming it batch-by-batch (Stream) produces
different end states (Fig.
[3](#S3.F3.fig1 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Experiment Set-up ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"));
updates on one task overwrite memory of another (Figs.
[8(b)](#S6.F8.sf2 "Figure 8(b) ‣ Figure 8 ‣ 6.2 Interference ‣ 6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
and
[8(c)](#S6.F8.sf3 "Figure 8(c) ‣ Figure 8 ‣ 6.2 Interference ‣ 6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"));
and a stream of repeated near-duplicates causes the memory to overfit to
seen instances and generalize poorly within the same task (Fig.
[11](#S7.F11.fig1 "Figure 11 ‣ 7 Conclusion ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
Meanwhile, an episodic-only control that consumes the same trajectories
without abstracting them—appending raw rollouts to context as in-context
demonstrations—is already competitive with the lesson-style
consolidators we test (Table
[4](#S4.T4.fig1 "Table 4 ‣ 4.2 An episodic-only store should be a diagnostic baseline ‣ 4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
Because the trajectory pool is held fixed across these comparisons, the
variance across schedules and the episodic-only control together point
to the consolidation step itself, not the underlying experience, as the
source of the failure.

We further identify three mechanisms behind faulty memory
(§[6](#S6 "6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
First, agents misgroup experiences before abstracting them, pooling
episodes that do not share underlying structure. Second, even when
grouping is correct, abstraction can strip the applicability conditions
of a lesson, so that overgeneralized entries interfere with neighboring
tasks. Third, when the input stream is narrow, abstraction overfits to
seen instances. Together, these failure modes weaken the boundary
between what should be generalized, what should remain task-specific,
and what should be preserved as raw episodic evidence ([Sun et al.,
2023](#bib.bib19); [Bartlett, 1932](#bib.bib2); [Brainerd and Reyna,
2002](#bib.bib3)).

Figure 2: Iterated stream consolidation collapses on solvable tasks.
GPT-5.4 accuracy on a 19-problem ARC-AGI slice it solves at $`100\%`$
without memory (dashed ceiling). Since ground-truth solutions are
available at every consolidation step, all input trajectories are useful
by construction. We compare Static, which consolidates the full pool in
one update, with Stream, which updates memory after each problem. Static
remains at the ceiling after $`R=10`$ and $`R=50`$ refresh rounds,
whereas Stream falls to $`52.6\%`$ by Round 10 on the same previously
solved problems.

These findings suggest a limitation in current LLM agents: while they
can often benefit from individual past episodes, they do not reliably
turn those episodes into stable and reusable abstractions over long
horizons. Many recent agentic-memory systems—CLIN ([Majumder et al.,
2023](#bib.bib5)), Agent Workflow Memory ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)), Dynamic Cheatsheet ([Suzgun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib29)), and ACE ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib24))—adopt
update-after-every-interaction designs that treat each consolidation
step as at worst neutral; our results contradict this assumption. For
today’s models, retaining episodes is the more robust default: when
ARC-AGI Stream agents are given retain, delete, and consolidate actions,
they preserve episodes by default and outperform their
forced-consolidation counterparts. Yet episodic accumulation cannot be
the long-term answer: as deployment continues, raw histories grow
unboundedly and resist compositional reuse—compression and transfer
ultimately require abstraction. We see faulty memory as a central open
problem in agentic memory, and our results motivate architectures that
keep the episodic and abstraction-forming roles distinct rather than
collapsing both into a single rewrite loop.

##### Memory in LLM agents.

LLM agents augment fixed-weight models with editable textual memory that
they themselves maintain. Across architectures, this memory takes many
forms: hierarchical context stores ([Packer et al., 2023](#bib.bib15);
[Letta, 2024](#bib.bib11)), reflective notes ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib18)), episodic streams ([Park et al., 2023](#bib.bib16)),
distilled lessons ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib6)), skill libraries
([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib22)), causal abstractions ([Majumder et
al., 2023](#bib.bib5)), dynamic memory stores ([Chhikara et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4); [Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [LangChain AI,
2024](#bib.bib10)), evolving playbooks ([Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24)), dynamic cheatsheets ([Suzgun et al.,
2026](#bib.bib29)), and reasoning memory banks ([Ouyang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30)). A popular paradigm is that LLMs abstract useful
procedural information from experience into text. This work mainly
concerns that category.

##### Schema formation and metacognitive control.

Cognitive theories of memory describe two complementary processes: a
fast episodic system that stores individual experiences, and a slow
process that extracts compact _schemas_—abstractions over many episodes
that integrate with prior knowledge to support future generalization
([McClelland et al., 1995](#bib.bib13); [Squire et al.,
2015](#bib.bib1); [Dudai et al., 2015](#bib.bib31); [Moscovitch et al.,
2016](#bib.bib32)). Schema formation is beneficial when new evidence
fits existing structure ([Tse et al., 2007](#bib.bib20)), but harmful
when it is non-selective or poorly controlled: nonselective
consolidation causes interference and loss of specificity ([McClelland
et al., 1995](#bib.bib13); [Sun et al., 2023](#bib.bib19)). Whether
consolidation helps therefore depends on _metacognitive
control_—deciding which experiences belong together, how abstractly to
rewrite them, and when to preserve distinctions rather than collapse
them. Human metacognition is itself imperfect ([Flavell,
1979](#bib.bib7); [Nelson and Narens, 1990](#bib.bib14); [Koriat,
1997](#bib.bib9)), and whether LLMs reliably monitor their
self-generated abstractions is an open question—in adjacent settings,
chain-of-thought explanations have been shown to diverge from the
underlying computation ([Turpin et al., 2023](#bib.bib21)). Agent-memory
systems implement an explicit analogue, abstracting “lessons” that are
reused on later tasks while putting the same model in charge of both
generating the memory and monitoring its own abstraction; the failure
modes we observe
(§[6](#S6 "6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
are consistent with this control loop being unreliable in practice.

##### Relation to catastrophic forgetting.

The degradation we study is related to but distinct from catastrophic
forgetting ([McCloskey and Cohen, 1989](#bib.bib12); [French,
1999](#bib.bib8))—the loss of earlier-task performance when a model is
trained sequentially on new tasks. Our failure is not induced by a
change of task distribution: it occurs with the task set held fixed
(repeated consolidation renders $`{\sim}46\%`$ of previously solved
problems unsolvable) and it manifests as _distortion_—merged task
families, over-generalized rules, confident-but-incorrect
procedures—rather than the fading of old knowledge. Consolidating the
same trajectories in one pass also beats streaming them, so the damage
comes from repeated rewriting rather than from the evidence. It
therefore calls for different remedies (gated, delayed abstraction with
preserved episodes) than the rehearsal or drift-regularization used
against catastrophic forgetting; we expand the comparison in
[Section L.4](#A12.SS4 "L.4 Relation to Catastrophic Forgetting ‣ Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs").

## 3 Experiment Set-up

Figure 3: Streaming consolidation collapses. Stream loses $`17`$–$`38`$
pts vs. whole-batch Pool.

We study how models abstract memory from experience across clean and
widely-used agent benchmarks—ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, AppWorld
([Trivedi et al., 2024](#bib.bib39)), and Mind2Web ([Deng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib38))—and a synthetic stream we built, _ARC-AGI Stream_, to
introspect the memory-management process under known task families and
ground-truth solutions.

We adopt representative agentic-memory methods that distill lessons from
past trajectories—CLIN ([Majumder et al., 2023](#bib.bib5)), Agent
Workflow Memory ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)), Dynamic Cheatsheet
([Suzgun et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)), and ACE ([Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24)).

##### Memory construction conditions.

Three regimes differ only in how trajectories are presented to the
memory manager: Static-All abstracts memory from the entire pool in
one-shot; Static-Group does so for each task type (for ALFWorld and
ScienceWorld) and concatenate: this simulates offline memory
construction and is used for control; Stream updates in batches,
simulating an agent that evolves continually. For Stream we change batch
size and within-batch task composition (homogeneous vs. heterogeneous)
and consider both unbounded and size-capped memory banks. At evaluation
we provide all memory entries in context and average two repeats per
question unless noted otherwise.

##### ARC-AGI Stream.

We introduce _ARC-AGI Stream_, a controlled testbed for introspecting
the abstraction process itself rather than only its downstream accuracy.
Building on ARCGEN ([Moffitt, 2025](#bib.bib40)), the testbed combines
three properties that, jointly, are absent from existing agent
benchmarks: _(i)_ a fully specified latent task taxonomy—following
ConceptARC ([Moskvichev et al., 2023](#bib.bib26)), each concept is a
distinct problem type, so memory-management actions (Fig.
[7(a)](#S6.F7.sf1 "Figure 7(a) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 6.1 Correct Segmentation Takes Time, Forced Abstraction Breaks It ‣ 6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
and results (Fig.
[6](#S5.F6.fig1 "Figure 6 ‣ 5 Mitigating Faulty Abstraction ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
can be traced family-by-family. _(ii)_ programmatic ground-truth and
_(iii)_ an exposed, structured vocabulary of memory operations whose use
we can audit per step. These controls make abstraction errors
attributable: if a model receives correct episodes from known families
but later merges families, the failure lies in memory abstraction rather
than others. Together they enable the family-coverage,
misclassification, and buffer-composition analyses in
§[6](#S6 "6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
that would not be measurable on ALFWorld/ScienceWorld/WebShop. Following
the Complementary Learning Systems framing ([McClelland et al.,
1995](#bib.bib13); [Sun et al., 2023](#bib.bib19); [Tse et al.,
2007](#bib.bib20)), we maintain two stores: an Episodic buffer of
problem –solution pairs and an Abstract store of consolidated lessons;
the control conditions below are designed to test this gating prediction
directly. At each step the model may Retain a raw episode, Delete an
entry, or Consolidate buffered episodes into the Abstract store; the
solver can be conditioned on either store or both stores. We compare
three control loops: Force requires consolidation each round and no
Episodic entries persist between rounds; Auto lets the model choose
whether to retain raw or abstract; Episodic Management Only allows only
retention and deletion, disabling abstraction entirely. Two trajectory
regimes complete the design: GT, where ground-truth solutions are
streamed to simulate training on demonstrations, and Running, where the
agent learns from its own attempts as it solves new problems. Prompt
templates are documented in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs");
the family and skill taxonomy used by the generator is in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Family and skill taxonomy [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs").

## 4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs

### 4.1 Stream Updates Reveal The Cumulative Effect Of Imperfect Abstraction

##### Abstracted memory utility is non-monotonic in updates.

Starting from an empty memory store, abstracted-memory utility rises
early and then falls below the no-memory baseline as updates accumulate.
Figure
[1(a)](#S1.F1.sf1 "Figure 1(a) ‣ Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
shows this curve on ScienceWorld with batches of 4 trajectories: the
score peaks near step 20 and declines through step 100 for every memory
size and sometimes below no-memory baseline. The same shape recurs on
WebShop, where AWM goes from $`0.64`$ at $`8`$ examples to $`0.20`$ at
$`128`$ while no-memory sits at $`0.20`$ (Fig.
[1(b)](#S1.F1.sf2 "Figure 1(b) ‣ Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))—scaling
the memory eventually erases its own benefit.

##### A strong memory is not a fixed point.

A high-quality starting memory does not stabilize under continued
consolidation either. We first consolidate ALFWorld trajectories with
GPT-5.4—the strongest model we test—following the Static-Group setting
from
§[3](#S3 "3 Experiment Set-up ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"),
then continue updating that store in batches with GPT-5-nano on the same
trajectory pool. Evaluated under three solvers (Qwen3.5-{27B, 9B, 4B})
to avoid idiosyncraticy, utility declines across all three solvers and
can drop drastically between consecutive evaluation steps (Fig.
[4](#S4.F4.fig1 "Figure 4 ‣ The consolidation procedure itself shapes the rate of decline. ‣ 4.1 Stream Updates Reveal The Cumulative Effect Of Imperfect Abstraction ‣ 4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).

##### The agent regresses on tasks it has already solved.

The cleanest, most striking instance is in-distribution regression on a
19-problem slice of the ARC-AGI Stream that GPT-5.4 solves at $`100\%`$
accuracy without memory. Streaming those same problems through the
consolidation loop, with ground-truth solutions available at every step,
brings GPT-5.4 down to $`54\%`$ on the very problems it had previously
solved (Fig.
[2](#S1.F2.fig1 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
Repeating the experiment ten times reproduces the drop, and on the
broader set of $`33`$ tasks the model solves without memory,
consolidated memory leaves a third of them unsolved by epoch 1 and
$`40\%`$ by epoch 10 (Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ The agent regresses on tasks it has already solved. ‣ 4.1 Stream Updates Reveal The Cumulative Effect Of Imperfect Abstraction ‣ 4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).

| GPT-5.4, ARC-AGI Stream (10 runs) | pass@1 (mean $`\pm`$ std) | pass@10            |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------ |
| No memory (baseline)              | $`58.5\pm 5.4`$           | $`100`$%  (33/33)  |
| Consolidated memory, epoch 1      | $`55.1\pm 4.9`$           | $`66.7`$%  (22/33) |
| Consolidated memory, epoch 10     | $`38.5\pm 5.3`$           | $`60.6`$%  (20/33) |

Table 2: The regression is not sampling noise, and it shows up as lost
coverage. Over ten end-to-end runs on the $`33`$ tasks solvable without
memory, consolidated memory leaves a third of them unsolved by epoch 1
and $`40\%`$ by epoch 10 (pass@10), while mean accuracy falls from
$`58.5`$ to $`38.5`$. The headline $`100\%\!\to\!54\%`$ in-distribution
regression thus survives repetition and an expanded task set.

##### The consolidation procedure itself shapes the rate of decline.

Figure 4: Heterogeneous batches accelerate erosion.

The decline is not driven by content alone; how trajectories are
presented to the consolidator changes the resulting memory in
content-independent ways. 1. Grouping by task family helps. Holding
update strategy fixed, consolidating each task family separately
(Static-Group) outperforms consolidating across families jointly
(Static-All - marked as Ungrp.); pooling heterogeneous tasks into a
single abstraction step invites confusion between unrelated procedures
(Fig.
[3](#S3.F3.fig1 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Experiment Set-up ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")). 2. One-shot consolidation beats streaming. Holding the trajectory pool
fixed, Streamed incremental updates underperform a single whole-pool
pass (Fig.
[3](#S3.F3.fig1 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Experiment Set-up ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
This suggests that early abstractions can anchor later rewrites and
mistakes are reused as context for future consolidation, so small errors
in segmentation or abstraction compound into progressively distorted
memories. However, in continual learning loops, memory gets repeatedly
updated as agents collect more experiences, instead of seeing the entire
pool of past interactions, precisely falling to the lossy update regime.

3\. Heterogeneous batches accelerate the decline within streaming. Even
when updates must be streamed, batches that mix tasks produce worse
memory than batches drawn from one task at a time (Fig.
[4](#S4.F4.fig1 "Figure 4 ‣ The consolidation procedure itself shapes the rate of decline. ‣ 4.1 Stream Updates Reveal The Cumulative Effect Of Imperfect Abstraction ‣ 4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")):
the model merges incompatible lessons inside a single update.

Figure 5: Cumulative success on ARC-AGI Stream across $`400`$ training
steps. Auto with a raw-episode buffer matches or beats both _Force_
(forced abstraction of every step) and the _No memory_ baseline on both
backbones.

##### Implications for memory design.

Each abstraction pass is a lossy rewrite that compounds over updates.
The pattern makes two predictions for how memory should be organized,
which
§[5](#S5 "5 Mitigating Faulty Abstraction ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
tests directly. (i) The raw trajectory logs that the consolidator
distills from should remain a competitive baseline, since they retain
what each rewrite discards. (ii) Allowing an agent to keep raw episodes
alongside (or instead of) abstracting them should outperform a regime
that forces every trajectory through consolidation.

general-purpose coding agent (OpenCode), at each backbone’s maximum

In WebShop, ALFWorld and AppWorld, an _episodic-only_ memory—append-only
trajectory rollouts in context, with no cross-trajectory abstraction —is
competitive with lesson-style consolidator we test (Table
[4](#S4.T4.fig1 "Table 4 ‣ 4.2 An episodic-only store should be a diagnostic baseline ‣ 4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs");
WebShop in Table
[6](#A0.T6.fig1 "Table 6 ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
in Appendix). The trajectory baseline stores the same experience that
ACE, AWM, and Dynamic Cheatsheet are asked to compress, and all memory
entries are placed in context at evaluation.

In most cases, abstracted memory cannot significantly outperform direct
in-context learning from trajectory logs (or subsets of them). It means
the evidence available before abstraction already contains task-relevant
signal that the solver can exploit directly: observations, actions,
intermediate failures, and environmental feedback remain tied to the
concrete situation in which they occurred. Schema-like behavior can
emerge from in-context learning on preserved instances comparative to a
separately stored abstraction ([Hintzman, 1986](#bib.bib33); [Brooks,
1978](#bib.bib34); [Medin and Schaffer, 1978](#bib.bib36); [Logan,
1988](#bib.bib35)). Therefore, we suggest that a memory method whose
value depends on distillation should be tested against the unabstracted
rollouts it distills.

## 5 Mitigating Faulty Abstraction

The findings in §
[4](#S4 "4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
imply experiences contain information the LLMs can consume for better
task performance, but the challenge is that those information fades with
repeated LLM updates instead of being refined.

Therefore, the memory architecture should be allowed to preserve
episodes instead of forcing every new experience through consolidation.
In this section, we present a controlled study to test whether granting
models autonomy of retention versus abstraction, and allowing parallel
stores of abstract and episodic memory would be a mitigation to the
effect.

ARC-AGI Stream lets us instantiate the two-process design explicitly.
The agent maintains both an Episodic buffer and an Abstract store, and
at each step may Retain, Delete, or Consolidate (Auto; cf. §
[3](#S3 "3 Experiment Set-up ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
We compare this to Force, where consolidation is required at every round
and no episodic entry persists between rounds. Three observations
follow.

First, the episodic store carries most of the gain. Removing episodic
evidence and using only abstract lessons collapses accuracy back to the
no-memory baseline (Fig.
[9(a)](#S6.F9.sf1 "Figure 9(a) ‣ Figure 9 ‣ 6.2 Interference ‣ 6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")),
indicating that the useful information was retained in raw episodes
rather than distilled entries.

Second, _Episodic Management Only_—retention and deletion of raw
episodes with abstraction disabled—matches or exceeds the full Auto mode
(Fig.
[9(a)](#S6.F9.sf1 "Figure 9(a) ‣ Figure 9 ‣ 6.2 Interference ‣ 6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
In this regime, the agent’s gains do not require an abstract store at
all.

Figure 6: Buffer composition over time on the ARC-AGI Stream

Third, forced abstraction underperforms retained-episode policies.
Across $`400`$ training steps, Auto—which keeps episodes by default and
uses abstraction sparingly—generally outperforms Force on both backbones
we test (Fig.
[5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ The consolidation procedure itself shapes the rate of decline. ‣ 4.1 Stream Updates Reveal The Cumulative Effect Of Imperfect Abstraction ‣ 4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
Whatever Force gains from compression, it can lose more by overwriting
evidence.

The agent’s own management decisions point in the same direction. Given
the option, it saturates the episodic buffer quickly at both budget
levels while keeping the abstract store sparse (Fig.
[7(b)](#S6.F7.sf2 "Figure 7(b) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 6.1 Correct Segmentation Takes Time, Forced Abstraction Breaks It ‣ 6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
The Auto-mode result therefore reflects an episodic-first policy that
the agent chooses when the architecture permits it.

##### Principle.

Episodic and schema-forming roles should not be collapsed into a single
rewrite loop. Complementary Learning Systems make this prescription
explicitly: a fast episodic store and a slow schema-forming store are
kept architecturally distinct so that fast learning does not overwrite
the slow one, and consolidation is gated by schema fit rather than
triggered on every event ([McClelland et al., 1995](#bib.bib13);
[Kumaran et al., 2016](#bib.bib25); [Tse et al., 2007](#bib.bib20); [Sun
et al., 2023](#bib.bib19)). The Force regime collapses this separation
into a mandatory rewrite loop, recreating the interference conditions
the dual-system design was meant to prevent ([McCloskey and Cohen,
1989](#bib.bib12); [French, 1999](#bib.bib8)). An episodic store should
therefore retain the evidence; abstraction, when it happens, should be
opt-in and gated by the agent rather than forced on every trajectory.

In our experiments, both policies that gate abstraction (Auto) and
policies that disable it entirely (Episodic Management Only) match or
exceed forced abstraction (Force), pointing to _mandatory rewriting at
every step_—rather than abstraction itself—as the decisive failure mode
in this regime ([Nelson and Narens, 1990](#bib.bib14); [Koriat,
1997](#bib.bib9)).

## 6 Failure Modes

We introspect three abstraction failures both quantitatively and
qualitatively: misgrouping before abstraction, interference from
overgeneralized lessons, and overfit to narrow streams of examples. We
present full case study results in
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs").

### 6.1 Correct Segmentation Takes Time, Forced Abstraction Breaks It

Correct segmentation—identifying which experiences belong together
before abstraction—is a precondition: an agent cannot abstract a lesson
from a set of episodes it has failed to group correctly ([Zacks et al.,
2007](#bib.bib41)).

The capacity for correct segmentation is in fact present. Given autonomy
over its memory, the model eventually converges to a clean episodic
store covering each of the 6 problem types(Fig.
[6](#S5.F6.fig1 "Figure 6 ‣ 5 Mitigating Faulty Abstraction ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
Yet the process takes time: only after 71 steps (568 examples) does the
model admit all six problem types into the buffer. In the Force regime,
where the model must consolidate at every step (8 fresh examples), it
makes mistakes frequently. Figure
[7(a)](#S6.F7.sf1 "Figure 7(a) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 6.1 Correct Segmentation Takes Time, Forced Abstraction Breaks It ‣ 6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
reports the _misclassification count_ — the number of memory-management
actions that combine episodes from two or more distinct problem classes
— and shows that, under forced consolidation, the model routinely merges
across class boundaries. The bottleneck is not recognizing class
structure but preserving it through cross-episode abstraction: the
forced act of abstraction overrides the segmentation the model is
otherwise capable of.

Each abstraction pass smooths and abstracts existing entries—a process
analogous to the semanticization of episodic memories under repeated
retelling ([Bartlett, 1932](#bib.bib2)); when the underlying chunks are

which a lesson applies, leaving what reads as broadly relevant when it
is not. On a related but different problem (Pick&Place versus
Pick-Clean-Place in ALFWorld), the agent sees these overgeneralized
lessons and is misled rather than aided (Fig.

### 6.3 Overfit

A complementary failure mode emerges when the input distribution narrows
rather than widens. In our ARC-AGI experiments, we repeatedly feed the
model tasks drawn from a single strategy family across consolidation
cycles. As the iteration count grows, the memory overfits to the
specific instances it has seen: performance remains stable on exact
repetitions of those problems but collapses on simple variations within
the same strategy family (Fig.
[11](#S7.F11.fig1 "Figure 11 ‣ 7 Conclusion ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs");
see
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
for case studies).

The abstraction loop, given a narrow stream, abstracts toward the
surface regularities of the observed instances rather than the
underlying problem-solving strategy.

### 6.4 What in the update does the damage?

Streamed consolidation could degrade for three separable reasons:
_initial compression error_ (information lost the first time a batch is
abstracted), _cross-update conditioning_ (earlier, imperfect
abstractions in context biasing how the next batch is consolidated), and
_destructive rewriting_ (editing entries in place erodes them
cumulatively). We separate them by streaming the same batches in the
same order while restricting only what the update step may see or do
(Table
[5](#S7.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 7 Conclusion ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
Forbidding in-place rewriting alone recovers most of the gap to raw
episodes; additionally hiding the prior store, so earlier abstractions
cannot condition later ones, recovers more still—yet none fully closes
the gap, because information is already lost at the very first
abstraction. All three mechanisms contribute and are separable: in-place
rewriting is the most damaging single component, while pruning (delete
without rewrite) actually helps. The full batch-size $`\times`$
update-mode grid is in
[Section L.2](#A12.SS2 "L.2 Attribution: Which Part of the Streamed Update Causes Degradation ‣ Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs").

## 7 Conclusion

Figure 11: Memory turns overspecified and hurt performance outside of
the compressed questions.

Persistent memory is meant to let LLM agents move beyond static
competence: experience is stored, compressed into reusable lessons, and
carried forward. We identify an issue that may undermine this promise —
across agent benchmarks and ARC-AGI Stream, continuously updated textual
memory can become less useful as experience accumulates; in the cleanest
case, an agent becomes worse on the very problems its memory was built
from.

| Streaming variant                        | What it removes vs. default        | Accuracy |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------- |
| Default consolidation (in-place rewrite) | —                                  | $`43.2`$ |
| Append-only, prior store visible (A)     | in-place rewriting                 | $`50.0`$ |
| Add + delete, no in-place edit (C)       | in-place rewriting (keeps pruning) | $`64.0`$ |
| Append-only, prior store hidden (B)      | rewriting _and_ conditioning       | $`70.0`$ |
| Raw trajectories (no consolidation)      | all consolidation                  | $`76.6`$ |

Table 5: The closer to raw episodes, the better—and in-place rewriting
is the most damaging single step. Accuracy on ARC-AGI Stream (GPT-5.4,
batch size 1, forced updates, step 400) as we strip components of the
streamed update. Forbidding in-place rewriting (A) recovers $`+6.8`$
over the default; also hiding the prior store so earlier abstractions
cannot bias later ones (B) recovers $`+26.8`$; adding pruning to
append-only (C) recovers $`+20.8`$. All remain below simply retaining
the raw trajectories the consolidator distills from. Full grid in
[Section L.2](#A12.SS2 "L.2 Attribution: Which Part of the Streamed Update Causes Degradation ‣ Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs").

The failure lies in the consolidation loop itself. Current LLMs do not
reliably decide which episodes belong together, which distinctions
should survive compression, or when an experience should remain
episodic. They misgroup trajectories, overgeneralize lessons, and
overfit to narrow streams. Because each update rewrites the products of
earlier updates, small abstraction errors compound into faulty memory.

These findings suggest that raw episodes should be treated as
first-class evidence, not disposable material to be compressed away.
Abstraction should be selective, delayed, and grounded in recoverable
trajectories. Until agents can control when and how to consolidate
experience, continuously updated textual memory should be treated not as
a reliable engine of self-improvement, but as a fragile mechanism that
can make more experience produce worse memory.

## Appendix A Family and skill taxonomy \[ARC-AGI\]

This section defines the two terms “family” and “skill” and lists the
six families and seven skills used in the ARC-AGI experiments.

### A.1 Definitions

Our task generator decomposes an ARC-style task along two independent
axes:

- •
  Family: a rule that selects the subset of connected non-background
  objects in the input grid that participates in the task’s
  transformation.
- •
  Skill: a fixed transformation applied to each selected object.

The two axes are orthogonal: the same family can be paired with
different skills, and the same skill can be paired with different
families. Some families are adapted from concept groups in ConceptARC;
for example, detect_inside_frame_relation corresponds to the
InsideOutside concept group.

### A.2 Family catalog

The six families span five distinct selection criteria: two are based on
intrinsic per-object attributes (color, size extremum), one on a global
conditional cue (a marker cell that triggers a branch), one on a
cross-object relation (shape-frequency mode), one on a spatial
containment relation (objects strictly inside a frame), and one on a
cross-grid structural property (a sub-scene of a two-panel input). The
chosen skill is then applied uniformly to whichever objects the family
selects.

| strategy_id                   | Selects by                | Definition                                                        |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| detect_color_property         | intrinsic (color)         | objects of a target color (inferred from the examples)            |
| detect_largest_objects_select | intrinsic (size extremum) | the largest object(s) by cell count (ties all selected)           |
| detect_key_marker_rule        | global conditional cue    | all-or-none global selection gated by the upper-left cell’s color |
| group_by_shape_then_select    | cross-object relation     | objects in the shape-frequency mode group                         |
| detect_inside_frame_relation  | spatial containment       | objects strictly inside a hollow frame                            |
| compose_horizontal            | cross-grid structure      | the left or right sub-scene of a two-panel input                  |

Table 8: The six families evaluated in this paper, grouped by what they
select on. The rightmost column gives the rule by which each family
picks the object subset that participates in the task’s transformation.
The first column reproduces the strategy_id field used to identify each
family in the released code and data.

Figure 12: One task per family, all rendered with the skill axis fixed
to recolor. Each panel shows two demonstration input–output pairs and a
held-out test input. Recolored objects in the output identify which
objects the family selects. Compose Horizontal takes two input grids per
example and transforms the left sub-scene; the other five families
operate on a single input. The Key Marker panel additionally illustrates
conditional branching: when the upper-left marker color matches the
trigger value, objects are recolored; otherwise the output equals the
input. Cell colors follow the 10-color ARC palette; color $`0`$ (black)
denotes background and colors $`1`$–$`9`$ denote object pixels.

### A.3 Skill catalog

Each skill applies a fixed transformation to every object in the
family’s selection.

| skill_id        | Definition                                                                   |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| keep            | Retain selected objects unchanged; erase non-selected objects to background. |
| border          | Draw a one-cell border around each selected object.                          |
| recolor         | Repaint each selected object in a single new color.                          |
| translate       | Shift each selected object by a fixed offset.                                |
| flip_horizontal | Mirror each selected object within its bounding box.                         |
| mark_center     | Mark the centroid cell of each selected object with a marker color.          |
| hollow          | Erase the interior of each selected object, leaving only its outer border.   |

Table 9: The seven skills evaluated in this paper. Each skill is applied
uniformly to every object selected by the family.

## Appendix B Prompts \[ARC-AGI\]

The experiments use three prompts: a solver prompt issued once per task,
a consolidator decision prompt that selects an action on the recent
history buffer after each passing step, and a consolidator extraction
prompt that produces a replacement strategy memory from a selected
subset of history. To make every field concrete we reproduce one full
step from a real run in which the current solve passes; the history
buffer carries two prior passing trajectories and strategy memory holds
one entry distilled at an earlier step. Each prompt is shown together
with the response it elicited. Where long content repeats across prompts
(the eight extra IO examples for the current task; the 8 tool-buffer
helper bodies; grids and solve code already shown above), we mark the
elision in square brackets; everything else is byte-for-byte from the
run logs.

### B.1 Solver prompt

The solver prompt is issued once per task at the start of the step. It
bundles the 10 IO examples for the current task, the existing strategy
memory, the tool-buffer helper signatures, and the recent history buffer
into one call.

### B.3 Consolidator decision prompt

After the solver’s response is graded passing, the consolidator decision
prompt is issued. The history buffer at this point contains three
entries: the two carryover trajectories shown in the solver’s history
block above, plus the trajectory just produced for the current task (one
IO pair plus the response above).

current strategy buffer is also supplied so the model can choose to
retain, merge, or drop existing entries.

### B.5 Failure recording prompt

whose solve was graded failing. Failed entries carry a Python-comment
banner that prepends the failed solve code with one input/output triple
from the failure: the input on which the candidate failed, the expected
output, and what the candidate produced. Because the banner is
comment-only, it is valid Python inside the same code fence the solver
prompt’s history block already uses. Below is one such entry from a real
run; the input grids were 16x16, abbreviated to the first four rows for
readability.

### B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt

An alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt asks the
model to emit a flat JSON list of strategies, where each entry is one of
three kinds: a retain (from_existing), a new pattern (strategy text plus
from_functions), or a merge that combines existing entries with optional
new evidence. Strategy text is a single free-form string rather than the
structured (when_to_use, solve_strategy) pair used in the prompt above.
We reproduce one full call from a real run; the buffer of existing
strategies was empty at this step, so the model returns one new entry
distilled from the single solve function shown.

##### Input.

`\iow_now:Ne``˝``\iow_now:Ne``˝Identify the high-level algorithmic strategies used in these functions (numbered 1 to 1).``\iow_now:Ne``˝Output the **FULL replacement strategy buffer** as a JSON list. Each output entry is one of:``\iow_now:Ne``˝- **Retain** existing strategies unchanged: “{"from_existing": [i, j, …]}“ –``\iow_now:Ne``˝ list any number of 1-based existing indices (the buffer is currently empty). Each listed``\iow_now:Ne``˝ index becomes its own kept-as-is entry in the new buffer (compact form for``\iow_now:Ne``˝ keeping several entries; equivalent to writing one “{"from_existing": [i]}“``\iow_now:Ne``˝ per index). Omit "strategy" entirely.``\iow_now:Ne``˝- **New** pattern extracted from the functions: “{"strategy": "<text>", "from_functions": [k1, k2, …]}“``\iow_now:Ne``˝ where “k*“ are 1-based indices into the functions below.``\iow_now:Ne``˝- **Merge** existing entries (and optionally new function evidence) into a single``\iow_now:Ne``˝ cleaner description: “{"strategy": "<merged text>", "from_existing": [i, j, …], "from_functions": [k, …]}“.``\iow_now:Ne``˝ Both index lists may have multiple entries; "from_functions" may be omitted if the merge is purely existing-only.``\iow_now:Ne``˝``\iow_now:Ne``˝Hard rules:``\iow_now:Ne``˝- Retain entries have NO "strategy" field and reference >=1 existing index. Multiple``\iow_now:Ne``˝ indices in one retain entry mean "keep all of them as separate entries".``\iow_now:Ne``˝- New / merge entries (with "strategy") MUST cite at least one source via "from_existing" or "from_functions".``\iow_now:Ne``˝- The difference between retain (multi-index) and merge: retain produces N separate``\iow_now:Ne``˝ entries unchanged; merge produces ONE new entry whose text is your "strategy" field.``\iow_now:Ne``˝- Existing indices not referenced anywhere in your output are dropped.``\iow_now:Ne``˝- Do NOT copy existing strategy text verbatim – use the index instead.``\iow_now:Ne``˝- You may output an empty list to drop everything.``\iow_now:Ne``˝Functions are numbered 1..1. ### B.7 Strategy selection prompt

An alternative invocation pattern for the solver decomposes the call
into a strategy-selection step followed by a synthesis step. The
selection prompt provides three inputs: the current callable helper
buffer, half of the task’s input-output examples, and the current
strategy memory. The model replies with a JSON object that names which
existing entry to apply; in the unconstrained variant it may instead
propose a new one. The selected strategy text is then injected into the
synthesis prompt’s memory block in place of the full memory listing. We
reproduce one full call from a real run; the helper-function bodies and
four of the five input-output example pairs are elided.

`\iow_now:Ne``˝``\iow_now:Ne``˝Choose a strategy for this task. Then choose how to proceed.``\iow_now:Ne``˝``\iow_now:Ne``˝ — 1. Tool buffer —``\iow_now:Ne``˝ Tool helper mode: direct_call. This task’s input-output examples —``\iow_now:Ne``˝ [Five 20x20 Input:/Output: example pairs elided – same format as in the solver prompt above.]``\iow_now:Ne``˝``\iow_now:Ne``˝ — 3. Currently existing strategies —``\iow_now:Ne``˝ 0. Extract connected objects, choose the largest as a frame, classify other objects by whether their bounding boxes lie strictly inside that frame, erase the frame and all outside objects, then hollow out each inside object in place by turning its interior to color 0 while preserving its boundary.``\iow_now:Ne``˝``\iow_now:Ne``˝ — 4. Choose strategy —``\iow_now:Ne``˝ Options (include a short "reason" in your reply). ## Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time \[ARC-AGI\]

### C.1 How a strategy is traced across compress steps

At each compress step we run the extraction prompt
([section B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"));
the consolidator returns the rewritten strategy memory as a JSON list.
Each list item declares its kind, one of three values:

- •
  retain — keep an existing entry from the current memory; the field
  from_existing lists 1-based indices into that memory.
- •
  new — distill a fresh entry from selected input tasks; the field
  from_functions lists 1-based indices into this step’s input tasks.
- •
  merge — emit a new entry that combines existing entries
  (from_existing) with new input tasks (from_functions).

Both kind and the two index fields come directly from the consolidator’s
JSON output. After parsing the response, we persist the resulting memory
as a per-step JSON snapshot; each entry in the snapshot carries this
step’s kind and its associated indices.

Because both merge and new produce a fresh entry rather than editing an
existing one in place, tracking how a strategy evolves over multiple
steps requires walking from_existing pointers backwards across
snapshots. Starting from a target entry, we look at its kind: if kind =
new, the chain has reached its root and the walk terminates; if kind =
merge, the index from_existing: \[j\] points to a predecessor in the
previous compress step’s memory; we look up the predecessor in the
snapshot we persisted for that step and take it as the new target. We
call a chain reconstructed by this procedure a _strategy lineage_.

### C.2 Worked lineage example

We ran GPT-5.4 on a 200-task pool spanning six ARC families, with the
same model serving as both solver and consolidator. We trace one
strategy lineage by the procedure of
[section C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 How a strategy is traced across compress steps ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"),
from its new step through its final merge, and show three snapshots: the
chain root, an intermediate node, and the chain’s final node. In the
latter two, yellow shading marks spans that differ from the previous
snapshot.

##### Chain root.

The chain begins with a new step: the consolidator distills four
inside-frame tasks into one entry.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Intermediate node.

Compared with the chain root: the horizontal-flip coordinate formula at
root step (7) is gone, the _When to use_ clause about mirroring is gone,
and a uniform-recolor step has been added in its place. The overall
scaffold — identify the frame as the largest object, classify other
objects by strict bounding-box containment, erase the frame and outside
objects, keep the inside objects — is preserved nearly verbatim.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Chain end.

Compared with the previous snapshot: the recolor step is gone, replaced

### D.5 Single-strategy collapse on multi-family compression

The cases above describe entries whose content is itself problematic.
This subsection describes a different failure with two parts: (i)
compression collapses multi-family training tasks into one single-family
playbook; (ii) retrieval applies that entry verbatim to held-out tasks
from other families. The entry text itself is internally consistent and
appropriate for its source family.

##### Example 1: 19 tasks revisited 10 times collapse to a single inside-frame plus hollow strategy.

We presented a fixed pool of 19 tasks, spanning the six families, to
GPT-5.4 10 times. The model viewed one task at a time alongside its
ground-truth solver code, and updated its memory after each task. After
10 passes (190 steps), the memory contained a single entry:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

On a held-out task whose true rule was “erase every object of one
specific color” — unrelated to the inside-frame pattern in the entry —
the same model produced:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The first comment reproduces the entry’s framing verbatim. The second
comment records the active color from the examples. The code below
treats color $`6`$ as the frame color rather than as the color to
remove. The code follows the entry’s frame-and-inside structure: it
picks a frame by size, copies only strictly-interior objects onto a
blank canvas, and hollows them in place. On this input no color-$`3`$
marker passes the strict-inside check, so the canvas stays empty. The
same model without strategy memory solved the task in eight lines:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![Refer to caption](2605.12978v2/case_task224_wrong_strategy.png)

Figure 14: Example 1, held-out task. The input contains a hollow
color-$`6`$ frame and several smaller color-$`3`$ markers. The same
GPT-5.4 solver passes this task without strategy memory (center, 10/10)
by erasing every color-$`6`$ component and keeping the markers; with
memory (right, 0/10) the solver instead executes the entry’s
frame-and-hollow playbook and produces an empty grid.

##### Example 2: 250 tasks streamed once collapse to a group-by-shape strategy.

In a separate run, we presented 250 training tasks to GPT-5.4 one at a
time, each paired with its ground-truth solver code. After each task the
model chose whether to update the memory. Training tasks again spanned
the six families. After 250 steps the memory contained two entries, both
from the group-by-shape family. Each entry prescribed partitioning
objects by translation-normalized shape signature, keeping the most
frequent signature class, and applying a decoration to the survivors.
The other five families (largest-object, color-property, key-marker,
inside-frame, compose-horizontal) had no entry in the memory.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

On a held-out task from the largest-object family — true rule “keep only
the largest connected component, erase the rest” — the same model with
this memory produced:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The solver transcribes the entry’s selection logic into Python:
signature() implements step (2), the dictionary count implements step
(3), and best_sig implements step (4). The downstream operation —
writing each kept object’s cells onto a blank canvas — is identical to
what the same model produces without memory, shown next:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Without memory the model identifies the correct selection criterion
(obj\["size"\] == max_size). With memory the selection criterion is
replaced by the entry’s signature(obj) == best_sig. The action that
follows the selection is unchanged. Replacing the selection criterion
alone, while keeping the action identical, drops the solver from 10/10
to 2/10 on this task’s 10 test grids.

![Refer to caption](2605.12978v2/case_task207_wrong_strategy.png)

Figure 15: Example 2, held-out task. The input contains one large unique
triangle (top-right), one medium unique H-shape (bottom-right), and two
small same-shape T-shapes (top-left and mid-left). The same GPT-5.4
solver passes this task without memory (center, 10/10) by keeping only
the largest object; with memory (right, 2/10) the solver keeps only the
two same-shape T-shapes, since the entry’s selection criterion is
shape-signature majority rather than size.

| Variant                  | generator  | per type | total | filtering                    |
| ------------------------ | ---------- | -------- | ----- | ---------------------------- |

Table 10: The three ALFWorld training-data variants differ on two axes:
total size (384 vs 768 trajectories) and reward filtering. The two
golden variants retain only success trajectories from gpt-4.1 rollouts;
with_failures retains both successes and failures from gpt-5-nano
rollouts and is used for probes that test consolidation behaviour under
imperfect inputs.

After collection, every raw trajectory is converted into a structured
memory item via the abstraction step of the SkillRL pipeline. We use
gpt-5.4 as the abstraction LLM. The abstraction makes 3 LLM calls per
trajectory and produces one item with three fields:
contextual_description, refined_trajectory, and strategic_guidelines.

#### Two-task-type probe set

For one probe experiment we use a focused training subset that pairs two
task types: pick_and_place (focal) and pick_clean_then_place_in_recep
(probe). The base memory at every probe point is a single-type
consolidation that fixes the per-stage task type to pick_and_place and
samples 32 abstracts per stage from the $`n{=}64`$ abstract pool;
snapshots are taken at consolidation stage $`S\in\{1,20,50,100\}`$. From
each snapshot we run one additional consolidation iteration with 32
abstracts. The management model is gpt-5-nano and it has a max capacity
of memory, which is 50.

#### Evaluation set

We evaluate on eval_id_balanced_48, a 48-episode subset of ALFWorld’s
in-distribution test split with 8 episodes per task type for the 6 task
types listed above.

#### Metric

Each ALFWorld episode has a binary success indicator (env reward $`=1`$
when the agent satisfies the goal within max_steps=50, else 0). We
report wins/48 (the count of successful episodes) and the corresponding
success rate in $`[0,1]`$ as the per-condition score on this evaluation
set.

We evaluate on test50_seed42_no_leak.json, a 50-session subset of
WebShop’s test pool (num_products=1000, seed $`=42`$) drawn from the
index range $`[0,500)`$. The 13 training-set session IDs (all from
Golden 128) that fall within $`[0,500)`$ are excluded from the sampling

#### Metric

Each WebShop episode terminates with a reward in $`[0,1]`$ computed from
attribute match between the purchased product and the instruction (a
perfect match yields reward $`1.0`$). If the agent never issues a
click\[Buy Now\] action and the episode ends without a purchase (e.g.,
the agent times out at eval_max_steps), the reward is $`0`$. We report
two quantities per condition: wins/50 (the count of episodes with reward
$`=1.0`$) and mean reward (arithmetic mean of episode rewards over the
50 evaluation sessions).

### F.3 ScienceWorld

We select 15 medium-difficulty tasks from ScienceWorld for the memory
consolidation experiments, where each selected task satisfies an average
optimal action sequence length between 20 and 100. In total, these tasks
contain 485 rollout cases. The task names and the number of rollout
cases for each task are shown in Table
[12](#A6.T12 "Table 12 ‣ F.3 ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs").

Our ScienceWorld experiments are based on the CLIN setting, with several
adaptations for studying long-horizon memory consolidation. Following
CLIN, each rollout is presented together with an evaluation report ⁽¹⁾,
which provides feedback about the success or failure of the
corresponding attempt. We also follow the CLIN-style constrained memory
format ⁽²⁾, where each memory is written as a unified natural-language
rule using one of a small set of relation phrases, such as MAY BE
NECCESSARY to, SHOULD BE NECCESSARY to, MAY BE CONTRIBUTE to, and DOES
NOT CONTRIBUTE to.

Compared with the original CLIN update procedure, we introduce several
modifications. First, we maintain a bounded memory bank and explicitly
inform the LLM of the maximum memory-bank size and FIFO replacement
policy, as highlighted in the memory-capacity instruction ⁽³⁾. Second,
instead of only adding new memories, we allow multiple memory-bank
operations, including delete ⁽⁴⁾, replace ⁽⁵⁾, add ⁽⁶⁾, and retain ⁽⁷⁾.
Third, we feed rollouts to the LLM in mini-batches and ask the model to
compare the buffered rollouts jointly before editing the memory bank, as
shown in the mini-batch consolidation instruction ⁽⁸⁾. Finally, after
each full pass over all rollouts for a given number of consolidation
rounds, we evaluate the current memory bank on a fixed ScienceWorld test
set. This test set contains 44 cases sampled from the same 15 selected
tasks, with 2–4 cases per task depending on the number of available
variants.

### F.4 AppWorld

#### Training data

We use 140 trajectories collected on AppWorld’s official train and dev
splits (Trivedi et al., 2024) as the shared training set across all
memory-induction methods evaluated in this work.

The 90-task train segment uses AppWorld’s officially released ReAct
baseline trajectories, produced with GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13). The
50-task dev segment uses ReAct trajectories collected with Qwen3.5-27B
on a stratified-by-difficulty sample of the dev split, run under
AppWorld’s standard ReAct interface. Composition is summarized in
[table 13](#A6.T13 "In Training data ‣ F.4 AppWorld ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs").
The mean Task Goal Completion (TGC) over the combined 140 trajectories
is $`61.4\%`$ ($`86/140`$): $`52.2\%`$ on the train segment and
$`78.0\%`$ on the dev segment.

For methods that require gold-quality input, we additionally collect a
parallel set of 140 trajectories on the same task IDs by replaying
AppWorld’s released ground-truth solutions through the environment API,
yielding a $`100\%`$-pass training set with identical task IDs and
ordering.

| Subset        | N   | Source split              | Trajectory backend |
| ------------- | --- | ------------------------- | ------------------ |
| Train segment | 90  | AppWorld train (90 tasks) | GPT-4o             |
| Dev segment   | 50  | AppWorld dev  (57 tasks)  | Qwen3.5-27B        |
| Combined      | 140 | —                         | —                  |

Table 13: Composition of the 140-trajectory AppWorld training set.

Each training datapoint consists of a task identifier, a final pass/fail
outcome, and a Qwen3.5-27B–generated prose summary of the full ReAct
trajectory (thoughts, actions, and observations of all steps), used in
place of the raw token-level trajectory to keep per-entry length
tractable for prompt-time concatenation.

#### Evaluation set

We evaluate on a 100-task subset drawn from AppWorld’s two official test
splits (test_normal with $`168`$ tasks and test_challenge with $`417`$)
by proportional stratified sampling on difficulty: 50 tasks from each
split, seed $`=42`$, with no overlap. All conditions are evaluated on
the same 100 task IDs.

#### Metric

Each AppWorld task is paired with a set of Python unit tests. The
official evaluator replays the agent’s trajectory against the resulting
database state and runs these tests; a task is counted as a success only
when all of its unit tests pass. Following AppWorld’s official protocol,
we report Task Goal Completion (TGC) as the sole metric: the percentage
of evaluation tasks whose success indicator equals one. All TGC values
reported in the main tables are arithmetic means over the 100 evaluation
tasks.

## Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes

### G.1 Erosion: good memory degrading over time

##### Setup.

The memory under study is produced by a 200-stage iterative
consolidation run on ALFWorld. The base memory at stage 0 is a 10-item
seed obtained by passing all 768 abstracts of the $`n{=}128`$ golden
ALFWorld training set
([section F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 ALFWorld ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
through a single gpt-5.4 consolidation call that emits a free-count list
of task-type-agnostic insights; the model picks the count, with no fixed
target. Each subsequent stage feeds gpt-5-nano a fresh mini-batch of
$`6`$ abstracts ($`1`$ per task type, drawn from the $`n{=}64`$ subset
of the same six-type pool) together with the current memory; the
management model rewrites the entire memory at every stage and forces
overwrites rather than appends. Besides, the memory capacity is 50. We
evaluate the consolidated memory at every 20 stages on the held-out
balanced ALFWorld split (defined in
[section F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 ALFWorld ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs");
n=48 episodes) using three Qwen3.5 sizes as rollout policies —

##### The erosion curve.

[fig. 16](#A7.F16 "In The erosion curve. ‣ G.1 Erosion: good memory degrading over time ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
plots wins/48 for the three rollout sizes at all evaluated stages,
against the corresponding no-memory baselines (15/48 for both 4B and 9B;
19/48 for 27B). All three sizes show the same qualitative pattern: an
early peak followed by a general decline (with small recoveries) to
stage 200. The 4B and 9B rollouts each gain a small bump at stage 20
(35/48 wins), then erode to 15/48 (4B) and 16/48 (9B). The 27B rollout’s
peak is at stage 0 (41/48), so for the 27B rollout consolidation never
helps; it erodes to 22/48 by stage 200. By stage 200 the gap to the
no-memory baseline collapses for the 4B and 9B rollouts ($`\Delta{=}0`$
and $`\Delta{=}1`$ respectively); the 27B rollout retains a
$`\Delta{=}3`$ gap above its baseline (22/48 vs. 19/48). Memory size
stays bounded at 38–50 items by the cap throughout, so the erosion is in
content quality, not item count.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 16: Iterative consolidation erodes the memory’s value across
three rollout sizes. By stage 200, the 4B and 9B rollouts collapse to
within $`1`$ win of their no-memory baselines (15 vs. 15; 16 vs. 15);
the 27B rollout retains a $`3`$-win gap above its baseline (22 vs. 19).
The 4B and 9B rollouts peak early (stage 20, 35/48 wins each) before
declining; the 27B rollout’s peak is the un-consolidated base seed at
stage 0 (41/48), so consolidation never helps it. Memory size is bounded
by max_memory_size=50 throughout, so the loss is in content quality, not
item count.

##### What is in the memory at the peak.

At stage 20 the 42 items each cover a distinct decision-relevant
insight. We reproduce items 0–5 verbatim below; items 6–41 expand on
this cover set with concrete recipes for heat/cool/clean tasks,
look-at-light tasks, and multi-object planning.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### What is in the memory after erosion.

At stage 200 the 38 items collapse onto a small number of overlapping
templates. By keyword scan, 22 of the 38 items mention the desklamp, 28
mention multi-object handling, and 33 mention systematic room-by-room
search; the templates overlap heavily (most items mention more than
one). Items 3 and 5 are byte-identical. The concrete meta-strategies of
stage 20 — the cooling-vs-heating asymmetry of item 3, the shuttle
default of item 5, the recognize-task-type-early principle of item 0 —
do not appear in concrete actionable form in any of the five
representative items below, and a full scan of the 38 items finds none

##### The collapse event.

At stage $`168`$ the memory contains $`50`$ items totalling $`48{,}506`$
characters (i.e., the cap is saturated, average $`\sim`$$`970`$
characters per item). One consolidation step later, at stage $`169`$,
the memory contains _a single item_ of $`1{,}960`$ characters. The
manager has merged $`50`$ structured items into one numbered “unified
loop” that tries to cover every ALFWorld task type at once. The collapse
is concentrated in this single stage. The preceding stage $`167`$ has
$`49`$ items; the following stage $`170`$ already begins to rebuild
($`2`$ items, $`3{,}410`$ chars).
