### G.3 Useless memory items

We distinguish two failure modes for memory items that are syntactically
well-formed but supply no decision-relevant information. Both modes
survive across stages because nothing contradicts them, and both consume
retrieval bandwidth without shifting the action distribution.

##### Overgeneralized.

Items whose recommendation applies to any state (“be careful”, “consider
all options”, “plan ahead”). The clause names no observable cue and
shifts no prior over candidate actions when retrieved.

We pull three verbatim items from an ExpeL iterative consolidation run
on ALFWorld ($`n{=}64`$ trajectories per task type, gpt-5.4 base model,
gpt-5-nano management, 200 mini-batch consolidation stages) at stage
$`200`$. The stage-200 memory has 9 active rules; we display the top-1,
top-2, and a low-vote item (Item 7, vote $`=2`$; the lowest is Item 8
with vote $`=1`$).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Worked example: how an ExpeL highest-voted insight collapsed.

The same run produced Item 0 above by repeatedly applying ExpeL’s EDIT
operation to the top slot. By stage $`200`$ the slot had accumulated
$`99`$ AGREE/EDIT votes, which would naively suggest extreme value. The
vote counter, however, increments on EDIT but is not reset when an EDIT
replaces the underlying concept. The score therefore tracks slot
edit-volume rather than current content quality. Tracing the slot
through stages, its content was rewritten through at least three
distinct concepts
([section G.3](#A7.SS3.SSS0.Px2 "Worked example: how an ExpeL highest-voted insight collapsed. ‣ G.3 Useless memory items ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The slot’s $`99`$ votes were earned across three different concepts
(examine-with-Y interaction $`\to`$ generic action selection $`\to`$
tautology). At stage $`200`$ only the third concept is in the slot; the
other $`\sim 80`$ votes were accumulated by predecessors that the EDIT
operation has since overwritten. The vote score is therefore not a
measure of the current rule’s value to the agent.

##### Overspecified.

Items so narrowly tied to a past trajectory state or to one (object,
surface, appliance) tuple that they cannot transfer once that condition
is not present. They survive in the cap because nothing contradicts
them; they take up retrieval bandwidth on tasks they do not match.

We pull three verbatim items from an ACE iterative consolidation run on
ALFWorld (6 abstracts sampled flat-randomly across all six task types
per stage; $`n{=}128`$ trajectories per type; analyzer dedup threshold
$`0.75`$; both reflector and curator $`=`$ gpt-5.4-mini). Each item is
an ADD operation recorded in the curator’s operation log. Reflector and
curator are the two ACE roles: the reflector emits bullet candidates
from each trajectory, the curator decides which are added to or modified
in the running memory, and the analyzer merges any pair of items whose
embedding similarity exceeds the dedup threshold.

#### H.1.1 Healthy snapshots: ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet

##### ACE healthy.

ACE keeps a flat list of bullet items grouped into named sections
(Common mistakes to avoid, Problem-solving heuristics). At stage $`100`$

contains $`32`$ bullets totalling about $`14`$k characters. We reproduce
one short bullet from each section.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Dynamic Cheatsheet healthy.

Dynamic Cheatsheet keeps a single living document and rewrites it after
every trajectory. The document at stage $`100`$ of the same run is
roughly $`8.3`$k characters, organised under a Action patterns and
interaction sequences heading with one \<memory_item\> per consolidated
insight (each with \<description\>, \<example\>, and a Count field). We
reproduce two consecutive \<memory_item\> blocks.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

These two snapshots illustrate the methods’ design intent: ACE produces
structured bullet lists with explicit failure-mode categories, while
Dynamic Cheatsheet produces one continuously-edited document with
embedded action templates and counter-examples. Both show concrete
domain content (apparel, sizes, colour names, price thresholds) and
avoid the empty-content / paraphrase failure modes of

## Appendix I Memory surgery

We isolate the contribution of individual memory items to overall
failure by removing one item from a memory snapshot and re-evaluating,
holding the rollout policy and all other items fixed.

### I.1 Workflow 8 ablation on WebShop

##### Setup.

The memory under study is a consolidated workflow file (8 workflows
W1–W8, reproduced verbatim in
[section I.1](#A9.SS1.SSS0.Px2 "The consolidated memory. ‣ I.1 Workflow 8 ablation on WebShop ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
produced after one epoch of AWM-style consolidation. AWM-style
consolidation abstracts each input trajectory into a workflow template
that pairs a thought rationale with an action sequence; we ablate
Workflow 8 (W8) of the resulting file. The training data are 128 expert
(task reward $`1.0`$) trajectories sampled from the AgentGym AgentTraj-L
WebShop corpus (seed $`42`$). The eval split is a 50-session subset of
WebShop’s test pool (seed $`42`$) with overlap to the training sessions
removed. We construct two evaluation conditions on this split:

- •
  Full memory: all 8 workflows.
- •
  Memory minus W8: the 7 workflows from the same file with Workflow 8
  removed (no other edits).

All conditions use eval_max_steps=30, eval_max_tokens=4096, and
eval_num_runs=1. We do not set a temperature parameter. Each condition
is evaluated under two rollout policies, gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5-mini.
The memory artifact is byte-identical across the two rollouts.

The WebShop action space used in
[table 16](#A9.T16 "In Behavioral evidence. ‣ I.1 Workflow 8 ablation on WebShop ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
groups raw click\[…\] actions into six categories by the type of UI
element clicked:

- •
  search: issue a query against the catalog, e.g., search\[red running
  shoes size 10 \< \$60\]. Returns a paginated list of product cards.
- •
  click ASIN: open a product detail page from a search-result card by
  its ASIN (Amazon Standard Identification Number, a 10-character
  product code such as b09npml43m), e.g., click\[b09npml43m\]. This is
  the only way to inspect a product’s variants, price, attributes, and
  Buy Now button.
- •
  click variant: select a required option on a product page before
  purchase, e.g., click\[medium\], click\[b16-red\]. Many products
  require one or more such selections; missing a required variant
  prevents reward 1.0 even if Buy Now succeeds.
- •
  click \[Next \>\]: advance to the next page of search results without
  opening any product, e.g., click\[Next \>\], click\[next &gt;\]. We
  also count the symmetric paging primitives click\[\< Prev\] here.
- •
  click back: return to the search input from a results or product page,
  e.g., click\[Back to Search\], abandoning the current query.
- •
  click \[Buy Now\]: commit to purchasing the currently configured
  product. Terminates the episode and yields the final reward in
  $`[0,1]`$ based on attribute match against the instruction.

##### The consolidated memory.

The full saved memory file contains 8 workflows, W1–W8, reproduced
verbatim below. The original file delimits each block with XML-style
\<think\> and \<action\> tags; we render them as italic
“Thought”/“Action sequence” labels for readability and otherwise
preserve the text. Highlighted spans in W8 key into the paired
annotations callout that follows.

##### Behavioral evidence.

With W8 in context, click\[Next \>\] dominates the action stream
relative to product-page interactions and click\[Buy Now\]. Removing W8
reduces this concentration in both rollouts (n=50 episodes per cell,
single run; no significance test). Under gpt-5.4-mini, observed
page-turn counts are $`421`$ (full) and $`181`$ (minus W8), a ratio of
$`2.3\times`$; the count of distinct episodes that issue at least one
click\[Buy Now\] is $`14/50`$ (full) and $`21/50`$ (minus W8). Under
gpt-5-mini, page-turn counts are $`559`$ and $`246`$ (also
$`2.3\times`$); the Buy-Now-episode count is $`28/50`$ and $`33/50`$.

## Appendix J ScienceWorld

### J.1 Abnormal memories

#### J.1.1 Representative cases

We first present three representative abnormal memory cases identified
in the ScienceWorld environment, one from each abnormality category.
These cases illustrate qualitatively different failure modes in memory
consolidation: over_generalization, where a memory abstracts from prior
experience too broadly and may bias the agent toward inappropriate
actions; over_specialization, where a memory is tied to overly specific
entities or procedures and therefore has limited transferability; and
useless_garbage, where a memory is vague, malformed, or insufficiently
actionable. For each case, we annotate the problematic components of the
memory and explain why retrieving it may hurt downstream
decision-making.

representative memory banks: the first round, which reflects the initial
memory bank; the tenth round, which reflects an intermediate memory
bank; and the twentieth round, which reflects the final memory bank. For
each memory bank, we also report the corresponding average test score.

## Appendix K Additional Analyses

### K.1 Auto-Mode Component Ablation

The main-text Auto + Episodic curve in Fig.
[9(b)](#S6.F9.sf2 "Figure 9(b) ‣ Figure 9 ‣ 6.2 Interference ‣ 6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
couples two memory sources. To isolate their contributions we re-run
evaluation at four checkpoints with each source restricted in turn:
Abstract Only reads only the distilled abstract memory, Episodic Only
reads only the raw episodic store, and Auto reads both. The Episodic
Only condition recovers nearly all of the Auto gain; Abstract Only never
improves on zero-shot (Fig.
[17](#A11.F17.fig1 "Figure 17 ‣ K.1 Auto-Mode Component Ablation ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).

Figure 17: What carries the Auto-mode gain? On the GT-400 stream, we
ablate which memory source conditions the solver at four checkpoints:
Abstract Only uses only distilled abstract entries, Episodic Only uses
only the raw episodic store, and Auto uses both. Episodic Only accounts
for nearly all of the gain; Abstract Only stays at or below the
zero-shot baseline (dotted) throughout; combining the two adds a few
extra points at every checkpoint but the late-step decline at $`400`$
tracks the abstract store’s gradual erosion.

## Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality

This appendix reports additional experiments that (i) attach variance
estimates to the headline results through repeated runs, (ii) isolate
_which_ part of the streamed-update procedure causes degradation, and
(iii) test whether the phenomenon survives stronger models, more memory
frameworks, longer contexts, and prompt optimization. Together they rule
out the three most natural alternative explanations for our central
finding—bounded-memory forgetting, context-window rot, and a single weak
implementation—and leave the consolidation step itself as the source of
degradation.

### L.2 Attribution: Which Part of the Streamed Update Causes Degradation

Streamed consolidation could degrade for three separable reasons: (1)
initial compression error—information lost the first time a batch is
abstracted, independent of any memory history; (2) cross-update
conditioning—earlier imperfect abstractions in context biasing how the
next batch is consolidated; and (3) destructive rewriting—repeatedly
editing entries in place erodes them cumulatively. We separate these
with three streamed conditions that see the same batches in the same
order and differ only in what the consolidation step may see or do
(Table
[22](#A12.T22 "Table 22 ‣ L.2 Attribution: Which Part of the Streamed Update Causes Degradation ‣ Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"));
results in Table

##### Reading the contrasts.

_Cross-update conditioning is real, but its sign depends on update
frequency._ At batch size $`1`$, hiding the prior store helps sharply
(Force $`50.0\!\to\!70.0`$ at step 400; Auto $`56.0\!\to\!66.0`$); at
batch size $`8`$ the effect reverses. This is expected if conditioning
carries both a cost—each imperfect abstraction biases the next update,
compounding over $`400`$ updates at batch $`1`$ versus $`50`$ at batch
$`8`$—and a benefit (seeing where new material belongs). Conditioning
therefore hurts specifically in the high-frequency regime where our main
result is observed. _Initial compression error persists even with
conditioning removed._ Condition B at batch $`1`$ is the strongest
streamed setting, yet $`70.0`$ still trails raw trajectories ($`76.6`$
ground-truth-code, $`70.4`$ natural-language; Table
[17](#A12.T17 "Table 17 ‣ L.1 Statistical Robustness under Repeated Runs ‣ Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")),
neither of which degrades over the stream. With no prior memory and no
rewriting, this residual gap can only be initial compression error.
_Removing conditioning is diagnostic, not deployable._ Unable to
deduplicate, condition B accumulates $`4.83\times`$ more entries and
$`3.81\times`$ more text than its visible counterpart at batch $`8`$,
eventually overrunning the context window (the missing step-400 cells).
_Rewriting damages memory; deletion does not._ Condition C beats A at
both batch sizes ($`66.0`$ vs. $`56.0`$ at batch $`8`$, Force, step 400)
with a smaller store, and both beat the rewrite-enabled setting at
matched batch size—C differs from A only by permitting removal, and from
rewrite-enabled only by forbidding in-place edits. Pruning helps; the
harm is specific to recursive in-place rewriting.

All three mechanisms contribute and are separable: initial compression
error is present even in the cleanest condition (B, batch $`1`$),
cross-update conditioning adds a penalty that scales with the number of
updates, and destructive rewriting adds a third, independent penalty.
This predicts the next intervention: fewer, larger updates should reduce
both the conditioning cost (fewer update events) and the compression
error (more reliable task-type segmentation), which
[Section L.3](#A12.SS3 "L.3 Delayed Compression Mitigates but Does Not Eliminate the Gap ‣ Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")
confirms.

### L.3 Delayed Compression Mitigates but Does Not Eliminate the Gap

Giving the consolidator larger batches (it sees $`32`$ examples at once
rather than $`8`$) raises terminal success (Table
[18](#A12.T18 "Table 18 ‣ L.1 Statistical Robustness under Repeated Runs ‣ Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
and roughly doubles the fraction of examples the agent chooses to
consolidate in autonomous mode (Table
[24](#A12.T24 "Table 24 ‣ L.3 Delayed Compression Mitigates but Does Not Eliminate the Gap ‣ Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
Both follow from broader within-batch evidence enabling more accurate
task-type segmentation—consistent with the finding
(§[6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Correct Segmentation Takes Time, Forced Abstraction Breaks It ‣ 6 Failure Modes ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
that whole-pool and task-grouped construction outperform incremental
streaming, and that heterogeneous batches merge incompatible procedures.
Delaying consolidation materially mitigates degradation but does not
close the gap to retaining raw experience.

| Batch size | Up to 100 | Up to 200 | Up to 400 | Ratio             |

### L.4 Relation to Catastrophic Forgetting

Our failure is related to but distinct from catastrophic forgetting (CF)
([McCloskey and Cohen, 1989](#bib.bib12); [French, 1999](#bib.bib8)),
the loss of performance on earlier tasks when a system is sequentially
trained on new ones. CF is induced by domain change and is standardly
mitigated by rehearsal/replay or regularization against drift. Our
degradation instead arises from the cumulative effect of imperfect
metacognitive chunking and lossy rewrites, on the same set of problems.
Four observations separate the two:

- •
  Degradation occurs with the task distribution held fixed. No new
  domain is introduced; repeated consolidation renders $`{\sim}46\%`$ of
  previously solved ARC-AGI Stream problems unsolvable—the agent loses
  ground on problems it has already mastered, which CF does not predict.
- •
  Mixing task types within a batch is worse than separating them
  (§[4](#S4 "4 Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"),
  Fig.
  [3](#S3.F3.fig1 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Experiment Set-up ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs")).
  Under CF, interleaving should _reduce_ forgetting; we observe the
  opposite, consistent with the consolidator chunking task types
  incorrectly over a mixed batch.
- •
  The same evidence produces different outcomes by arrival order.
  Consolidating a stream incrementally is worse than consolidating the
  identical trajectories in one pass, so the damage comes from repeated
  rewriting rather than from what the evidence contains.
- •
  The corruption is distortion, not loss. Inspecting the stores
  ([Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
  we find merged task families, procedures over-generalized past their
  scope, confident-but-incorrect procedures, and deleted
  exceptions/conditionals. CF predicts old knowledge fading; here memory
  instead accumulates assertions that were never true.

The degradation is therefore a distinct failure mode that calls for
different mitigations (gated, delayed abstraction with preserved
episodes;
§[5](#S5 "5 Mitigating Faulty Abstraction ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
than rehearsal or drift regularization.

### L.5 Context Length Is Not the Cause

Because consolidation is a procedural-memory mechanism rather than
context-window compression, we test directly whether extreme context
length, rather than faulty abstraction, drives the collapse. We pad the
ARC-AGI Stream prompt with randomly sampled training problems—first
_without_ solutions (length but no usable signal; Table

### L.6 Generality Across Models and Memory Frameworks

The degradation is not specific to the four consolidation methods or the
backbones in the main text. We extend to seven published memory
frameworks with an additional backbone (Claude Sonnet 5) and to a
general-purpose coding agent (OpenCode) given full autonomy over memory
management at maximum reasoning budget.

### L.7 Prompt Optimization Does Not Overcome It

The consolidation comparison is already prompt-controlled: Static and
Stream use the same solver and consolidation prompt, yet whole-pool
consolidation stays at $`18/19`$ while incremental consolidation falls
to $`10/19`$ on the regression slice. To test whether prompt engineering
can _recover_ a collapsed memory, we applied GEPA (reflective prompt
evolution) to the streamed epoch-10 configuration. GEPA recovers part of
the loss ($`47.9\!\to\!66.3`$; Table
[29](#A12.T29 "Table 29 ‣ Seven frameworks, two backbones. ‣ L.6 Generality Across Models and Memory Frameworks ‣ Appendix L Extended Experiments: Robustness, Attribution, and Generality ‣ Appendix K Additional Analyses ‣ J.1.3 Memory banks across consolidation rounds ‣ J.1.2 Additional examples ‣ J.1 Abnormal memories ‣ Appendix J ScienceWorld ‣ Appendix I Memory surgery ‣ Appendix H WebShop ‣ Appendix G Case studies of memory failure modes ‣ Appendix F Additional Experiment Details ‣ Appendix E Examples of useful / well-formed strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix D Examples of wrong / low-quality strategies [ARC-AGI] ‣ Appendix C Strategy memory evolution over time [ARC-AGI] ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.7 Strategy selection prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.6 Alternative schema for the consolidator extraction prompt ‣ B.5 Failure recording prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.4 Consolidator extraction prompt ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.3 Consolidator decision prompt ‣ B.2 Tool helper bodies ‣ Response. ‣ Input. ‣ B.1 Solver prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompts [ARC-AGI] ‣ Useful Memories Become FaultyWhen Continuously Updated by LLMs"))
but does not overcome the effect. Tellingly, the selected prompt does so
by cautioning the model _against_ relying on the memory:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Across diverse frameworks, frontier models, unbounded memory, extreme
context, and prompt optimization, repeated consolidation can erase
useful knowledge—so the failure is not attributable to one weak
abstraction method, a fixed memory budget, or an ineffective prompt.
